# botmux 文档

> 飞书话题群 ↔ AI 编程 CLI 桥接

## Other

- [About & Resources](/botmux/en/about.md): botmux connects Lark topic groups to AI coding CLIs (Claude Code, Codex and more): start a topic in a group and you get a dedicated AI session working for you. It's open source under the MIT license.
- [Multi-CLI Adapters](/botmux/en/adapters.md): botmux is not tied to one AI coding tool. Each bot picks the CLI / agent it runs with cliId, and the adapter delivers Lark messages to it and brings the replies back. Switching CLIs means changing one field. Local CLIs: every session is a real process on this machine. Under the default tmux backend you can tmux attach and watch it directly (pty / zellij / herdr backends differ).API / remote agents: a few adapters (e.g. Mira App, riff, Remote Runner) don't start a local CLI process; they call a remote service. For minimal configs see API / remote adapters. Use this page when: you want to switch the underlying CLI, wire up a new tool, or check whether a CLI accepts a model. No new adapter needed: for gateways / launchers (aiden, ttadk, ccr, …) see Wrapper / gateway integration; for strictly Codex-compatible distributions see Codex-compatible distributions.
- [Session Adopt](/botmux/en/adopt.md): Your CLI is halfway through a task and you have to leave? Send /adopt in Lark to bring that already-running CLI into the current topic: watch progress and keep sending messages from your phone, and find everything unchanged when you're back at your desk. Supported terminals: tmux, Zellij, Herdr, and Orca (experimental). The same card also lists past sessions of the bot's CLI, so you can resume one into the current topic. <video src={video_v3_adopt_relay_en} controls preload="metadata" style={{width:'100%',borderRadius:'8px'}}></video>
- [Core-only (apiOnly) API Control](/botmux/en/api-core-only.md): Want to embed botmux in your own system and drive a CLI over HTTP, without touching Feishu? Use core-only.It is botmux as one process, on a fixed port, listening only on 127.0.0.1: no Feishu credentials, no bots.json, no supervisor or dashboard. Your orchestrator (task runner, CI, backend service, sandbox) asks it over HTTP to run a CLI (codex / claude-code / …), polls the result, and opens a web terminal when it needs to see what's happening. This page is for integrators embedding botmux into their own product, for example a botmux inside a sandbox running codex. If you only want an external system to trigger a normal bot already running in a Feishu group, see Triggering Tasks via API. The two pages complement each other: the request body, idempotency and polling states work exactly the same under core-only. This page only covers what's specific to core-only: startup, readiness, interrupting a turn, the web terminal, auth, and the security boundary. Two related entry points: to start sessions and fetch results from a local script or CI, use Headless Automation Sessions; to let OpenAI-protocol tools reuse a CLI's model login, use Model Proxy (it runs a core-only instance underneath).
- [Trigger botmux Tasks via API](/botmux/en/api-task-trigger.md): Want an external system (task orchestrator, CI, backend service…) to hand an instruction to a botmux bot and get the result back programmatically? Use POST /api/trigger. The bot runs its CLI as usual; the task can stay entirely out of Feishu, or land in a real group or thread. This page is for client developers. The first three sections cover the common case; the rest is the full reference for fields, status codes and edge cases — look things up as you need them.
- [Architecture overview](/botmux/en/architecture.md): <video src="../img/video-v9-architecture-en.mp4" controls preload="metadata" style="width:100%;border-radius:8px"></video> What botmux does fits in one sentence: it turns Lark messages into input for an AI coding CLI, and turns the CLI's output back into Lark cards. This page covers which processes make up botmux, how a message flows through them, and what happens on restart. You don't need any of this for day-to-day use; come back when you're troubleshooting or contributing.
- [Best Practices](/botmux/en/best-practices.md): Recommended setups organized by use case; each item is something you can do right away. For feature details see the individual pages; if something goes wrong, start with Common pitfalls and the FAQ.
- [bots.json Configuration](/botmux/en/bots-json.md): ~/.botmux/bots.json is the bot configuration file. It is an array, and each entry is one bot. Each bot runs in its own daemon process. larkAppId and larkAppSecret are all you need to get started. Every other field is optional; add them as you need them.
- [Streaming Cards](/botmux/en/cards.md): <video src="../img/video-v2-daily-en.mp4" controls preload="metadata" style="width:100%;border-radius:8px"></video> Botmux uses Lark cards to show what the CLI is doing, and lets you control it right from your phone. This page goes from most common to advanced: first what shows up during a turn, then the status card, dynamic single cards and the switches, and finally the features for scripts and integrators.
- [CLI Commands](/botmux/en/cli-commands.md): botmux commands come in two kinds: Operator commands: you run them in a server terminal to manage the daemon (the background process), bots, and sessions.In-session commands: the AI calls them inside a session to send messages, read history, create scheduled tasks, and so on. You usually don't type these yourself. If you forget an option, run botmux --help for an overview, or botmux <subcommand> --help for the full options of one command.
- [Local Companion API](/botmux/en/companion-api.md): The Companion API is a small, local-only interface. It lets your own tools on the same machine (test scripts, a desktop companion app, and so on) read and change two things on one test Bot: Role: the Bot's default role (persona) and how it is injected;Runtime: which CLI it uses (Codex or TRAE), which model, and which reasoning level. It is off by default. When on, it is bound to the single Bot you name at startup. It does not reuse Dashboard login tokens and cannot proxy any other Dashboard route.
- [Dashboard Control Panel](/botmux/en/dashboard.md): <video src="../img/video-v7-dashboard-en.mp4" controls preload="metadata" style="width:100%;border-radius:8px"></video> The Dashboard is botmux's built-in web admin console. One page lets you manage sessions, groups, scheduled tasks, workflows, and configuration for every bot on this machine, without typing commands into each Lark group.
- [Decision Board and Steward](/botmux/en/decision-board.md): Make one bot your steward: you hand it development tasks and it pushes them forward in the relevant chats. Anything that needs your call goes onto the decision board. You write a decision per item (screenshots welcome), click Submit once, and the whole batch reaches the steward as one message. The steward executes it item by item and writes the results back to the board. Off by default. Bots without a steward get no extra files, pages or prompt text.
- [macOS Desktop App](/botmux/en/desktop.md): Botmux Desktop is the Mac app for botmux. It ships with its own runtime, so you don't need Node or a global botmux command. Double-click it to start the background service, browse the Dashboard, and read logs. It's a good fit when: You run botmux on a Mac and want a window with start / stop buttons instead of remembering commands.You'd rather not deal with Node versions on your machine.You want botmux to start in the background when you log in to your Mac. For Linux servers or dev boxes, keep using the command-line install in Quick Start. The desktop app is macOS only.
- [Feishu Doc Comment Watching (/watch-comment)](/botmux/en/doc-comment.md): Let the bot "live" in a Feishu/Lark cloud doc: ask a question or make a request in a doc comment, the AI reads the doc and does the work, then posts its answer straight back into that comment's thread. No need to leave the doc or switch to a group. Good for: Asking "does this section match the code?" while reading a design docHaving the AI rewrite, extend, or review a passage in the docLetting the AI pre-read a doc before a meeting, so everyone can ask in comments during the meeting
- [Environment Variables and File Locations](/botmux/en/env.md): Most settings live in bots.json and the Dashboard, so you usually don't need environment variables. Only a few machine-wide switches (bind address, ports, external address, backend type, and so on) go in ~/.botmux/.env. This page lists those switches and where botmux keeps its key files, for backup and troubleshooting. When to read this page: the Dashboard or web terminal won't open, you need to change a bind address or port, terminal links show the wrong address, you want the pty backend, or you're looking for config / logs / data. This page covers botmux's own processes. To control which variables the CLI inside a session receives, use the Dashboard: "Settings → Session environment" (global) or "Bot settings → Advanced → Startup environment → Session environment" (per bot). See bots.json → Session environment.
- [FAQ / Troubleshooting](/botmux/en/faq.md): Collected from the README and frequent questions in the community group, and updated over time. For more pitfalls, see Common Pitfalls. This page is grouped by topic:
- [Feedback Storage & Migration](/botmux/en/feedback-storage.md)
- [Global Settings (config.json)](/botmux/en/global-settings.md): Some switches apply to the whole machine, not to one bot: when to auto-update, whether to clean up idle sessions on a schedule, who gets pinged when the host is overloaded. They live on the Dashboard's "Global Settings" page. Saving writes them to ~/.botmux/config.json, shared by every bot on this machine. To change a single bot (working directory, admins, CLI, and so on), see bots.json. For environment variables used inside sessions, see Environment Variables.
- [Create a Session Group in One Step](/botmux/en/group.md): <video src="../img/video-v4-multibot-en.mp4" controls preload="metadata" style="width:100%;border-radius:8px"></video> Want a clean group dedicated to one project or task? Send /group <group name> (short form /g). The bot will: Create a new Lark group and add you to it;Transfer group ownership to you;Reply with a card containing the join link. Open the group and start talking to the bot. The whole group is one independent CLI session (a session is one running AI coding CLI process, such as Claude Code or Codex). The reply looks roughly like: Creating the group does not start a session. The session starts when you send your first message in the new group. botmux has two kinds of "session group". This page covers both:
- [Headless Automation Sessions](/botmux/en/headless-session.md): botmux session lets scripts, CI jobs, or scheduled jobs start an AI session without a Feishu group: send a prompt, wait for it to finish, and read the result. When people need to see it, one command publishes the session to a new group or binds it to an existing group / topic, and the conversation continues in Feishu. Good fits: In CI, let the AI review code first, and only open a group to notify people when something is wrong;Run batch analysis from a script when you only want the text result and no chat noise;Do the investigation in the background, then hand the team "the existing context + a summary" in one go. How the two command sets relate: botmux session is the stable, automation-facing entry point; botmux headless is the layer underneath. Prefer session in scripts. Use headless when you need finer control (for example, post one turn's result without moving the session).
- [Lifecycle Hooks](/botmux/en/hooks.md): Hooks let botmux run your own command at key moments: a new topic arrives, a session starts or exits, something needs a human, a turn finishes… Use them to send notifications, keep audit logs, auto-update skills, or run a custom check before a message reaches the CLI. There are two kinds of hooks:
- [Mention Policy (`mention-mode`)](/botmux/en/mention-mode.md): In a regular group, the bot by default answers only messages that explicitly @-mention it. The mention policy decides when you can skip the @. It only decides "is this message calling this bot?" — it does not grant permissions. Skipping the @ never skips authorization: people without talk access are still blocked (see Permissions & Authorization).
- [Model Proxy (Experimental)](/botmux/en/model-proxy.md): ⚠️ Experimental: endpoints, fields and limits may change. It does not affect regular Feishu bots. botmux model-proxy serve starts an authenticated, OpenAI Chat Completions–compatible endpoint on 127.0.0.1. Tools that only speak the OpenAI protocol (scripts built on the OpenAI SDK, code-review tools, and so on) can point their baseURL here and call models through a CLI's own login (Codex, Claude Code, …) — no separate API key needed.
- [Multi-bot Collaboration](/botmux/en/multi-bot.md): You can run several Lark bots on one machine, each backed by a different CLI (say, one Claude Code and one Codex). Put them in the same group and different models can work together and pick holes in each other's work. <video src={video_v4_multibot_en} controls preload="metadata" style={{width:'100%',borderRadius:'8px'}}></video>
- [Multi-Topic Orchestration Mode](/botmux/en/multi-topic.md): <video src="../img/video-v4-multibot-en.mp4" controls preload="metadata" style="width:100%;border-radius:8px"></video> Hand a big task to a main bot and it will: split the task into a few sub-projects;open a child topic in the group for each sub-project and send a group of bots in to work in parallel (a common pairing: one writes code, one reviews);use a Lark task checklist as the shared progress board;collect the results when every group is done and summarize them for you. An ordinary group turns into a parallel workbench. It builds on multi-bot collaboration.
- [On-Call Mode](/botmux/en/oncall.md): <video src="../img/video-v6-oncall-voice-en.mp4" controls preload="metadata" style="width:100%;border-radius:8px"></video> Add a bot to a duty, alert, or Q&A group and bind it to a project directory. From then on anyone in the group can @ it with a question. No repo picker, no access request: the bot answers from that directory. It fits groups where "lots of people ask, at any time, about the same project": duty groups, alert groups, cross-team Q&A groups. Adding the bot to a group does not open it up. Everyone in the group can talk to it only after an on-call binding (or after a bare /grant opens the whole group). Without either, a non-listed member who @-mentions it is blocked and gets a grant request card. See Permissions & Access · Being added to a group is not authorization.
- [Permissions & Authorization](/botmux/en/permissions.md): botmux permissions answer just two questions: Most ways of granting access give talk only. Operate rights belong to admins (allowedUsers) by default.
- [Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them](/botmux/en/pitfalls.md): Problems that keep coming up in the community, roughly ordered by how common they are. If something misbehaves after installing or upgrading, scan this page first — it is most likely a known issue. Not sure where to start? Jump to General troubleshooting approach at the end.
- [Central Platform (Open Source)](/botmux/en/platform.md): The open-source, self-hosted central platform for botmux: sign in with Lark, manage every machine in one website, open Dashboards and terminals remotely, and work with a team.
- [Plugin Development and Publishing](/botmux/en/plugins.md): A Botmux plugin is one npm package. Once installed, it can give the Agent Skills and MCP tools, add subcommands to the botmux CLI, add a page to the Dashboard, run a long-lived background service, and register Feishu /slash commands and card buttons. Start with what you want to do: Installing a third-party plugin means trusting its author: plugin code runs as the system user that runs Botmux. Confirmed Dashboard installs skip npm lifecycle scripts; ordinary CLI installs may still run them. Only install packages you trust. A catalog listing is not a security endorsement.
- [Prerequisites](/botmux/en/prerequisites.md): Before installing botmux, take a minute to check the items below. Most "installed but won't connect" or "sessions won't start" problems come from something missing here: the CLI isn't logged in, tmux isn't installed, or a command isn't on PATH. Read this if: you'll run the botmux daemon (the background process) on your own machine (dev machine / devbox / server).Skip this if: you only @ a bot in a group someone else already set up. You don't need to install anything locally.
- [Project Progress Card](/botmux/en/project-card.md): When you drive a multi-step project in an ordinary group, the coordinator bot can use botmux project to keep a pinned project progress card: goal, current focus, to-dos, blockers, milestones and the status of every subtask, all on one card that is updated in place instead of flooding the chat. Project state is stored on the host, not in chat history. If someone withdraws the card, the next update posts a new one and pins it again.Subtasks the coordinator sends out with botmux dispatch are registered on the card automatically, and progress that worker bots send back with botmux report is synced to the same card.One group has one project and one card. These commands are usually run by the AI itself. You tell the coordinator in the group "start project X" or "record that blocker", and it runs the matching command. The reference below helps you understand what it is doing; you can also ask it to run a specific command.
- [5-minute quick setup](/botmux/en/quickstart.md): <video src="../img/video-v1-quickstart-en.mp4" controls preload="metadata" style="width:100%;border-radius:8px"></video> Four steps and you're chatting with an AI coding CLI from Lark: Before you start: take a quick look at the Prerequisites. The CLI you want to use (e.g. claude, codex) must already be installed, signed in, and working in a terminal; tmux is also needed by default. Most "installed but won't connect" problems come from something missing here.
- [Session Relay](/botmux/en/relay.md): <video src="../img/video-v3-adopt-relay-en.mp4" controls preload="metadata" style="width:100%;border-radius:8px"></video> /relay moves a running AI session to another group, another topic, or a DM, so you can keep going there. What moves is the same CLI process and the same AI memory, not a fresh copy.The Lark chat history stays where it was. The new place won't show the old messages, but the AI remembers what was discussed. A typical case: work out a plan in your DM with the bot, then move it into the team group with one command so everyone continues from that context. How it differs from Adopt: Adopt brings a CLI running in tmux on your computer into Lark. Relay moves a session that's already running inside botmux from place A to place B.
- [Roles and Teams](/botmux/en/roles.md): Give a bot a "persona" (Role): who it is in the group, what it's responsible for, and how it talks. The same bot can play different roles in different groups. The command is /role. What's on this page:
- [File & Network Sandbox](/botmux/en/sandbox.md): The sandbox limits what the CLI behind a bot can touch on your host: it keeps secrets out of reach and stops the CLI from wrecking your environment. It is configured per bot and works on both Linux and macOS.
- [Scheduled Tasks](/botmux/en/schedule.md): <video src="../img/video-v5-automation-en.mp4" controls preload="metadata" style="width:100%;border-radius:8px"></video> Let a bot do work on a schedule: a daily morning report, a service check every 30 minutes, cleaning up a branch once a PR merges. When a task is due, the bot hands your prompt to its AI CLI and posts the result back to Feishu/Lark.
- [Session & Topic Model](/botmux/en/session-model.md): In botmux, a session = one running AI coding CLI process (such as Claude Code or Codex) + its context. Every message you send lands in some session. Questions like "why does every @ feel like starting over" or "why can't a new group see earlier chat" all come down to which session a message landed in. This page explains that, and how to start, continue, and recover sessions.
- [Skill + CLI Interaction](/botmux/en/skill-cli.md): <video src="../img/video-v8-skills-en.mp4" controls preload="metadata" style="width:100%;border-radius:8px"></video> Inside a botmux session, the AI talks to Lark (sending messages, reading history, creating scheduled tasks…) through two things: The botmux command: added to the CLI's PATH when the session starts. The AI just runs it in the terminal.Skills: short SKILL.md guides that tell the AI when to use which command and how. So when "the terminal shows output but nothing reaches Lark", the AI usually didn't run botmux send. See FAQ · C.
- [Slash Commands](/botmux/en/slash-commands.md): Just send these commands directly in a topic, and the daemon intercepts and handles them. Only the allowlisted commands in the passthrough section are forwarded verbatim to the underlying CLI; any other /xxx the daemon doesn't recognize is treated as ordinary conversation text and relayed as a normal message. Send /help anytime to view the full list.
- [Tmux Session Persistence](/botmux/en/tmux.md): A "session backend" is how botmux hosts the CLI process. The default backend is tmux: each topic's CLI runs inside a tmux session, so when botmux itself restarts, the CLI keeps running. So the most common question, "will restarting botmux lose my context?", has a simple answer: no.
- [Stop sending when the topic is unavailable](/botmux/en/topic-unavailable-policy.md): While the AI is working in a topic, someone may withdraw the original topic message. By default, Botmux keeps its existing delivery rules: for example, if the quoted message was withdrawn, the reply is posted to the top level of the chat instead. If you don't want replies to "move somewhere else", turn on the Stop sending policy for the bot. Before each send, Botmux checks that the original topic still exists. If it is gone or can't be verified, nothing is sent, and nothing is redirected.
- [Turn Results (TurnResult)](/botmux/en/turn-results.md): After a bot answers a question in Feishu, a program on the same machine can call one endpoint to get a structured result for that turn: did it finish, what was the final answer, and was it actually delivered to the chat. The endpoint is read-only. It does not rerun the model, send messages, or perform any business action for you. Typical uses: A host program on the same machine wants to know "what did the bot answer to that message, and did it arrive?"You want to feed the bot's final answer into your own pipeline (archiving, post-processing) without parsing chat messages. To start a task from outside and get its result, use the trigger APIs in Webhook or Core-only API. This page only covers reading results from ordinary Feishu conversations.
- [Voice Summary and Speech Recognition](/botmux/en/voice.md): botmux voice works in two directions. Turn on either one, or both: Both are optional advanced features, off by default. Run botmux restart after configuring them.
- [Web Terminal (interactive)](/botmux/en/web-terminal.md): <video src="../img/video-v2-daily-en.mp4" controls preload="metadata" style="width:100%;border-radius:8px"></video> Every session has a browser-based terminal: open it to watch the CLI live, and if you have permission, type into it directly. It works on desktop, tablet, and phone. The one exception is the ZMX backend, which has no Web Terminal. Run botmux list or zmx attach on the host instead; see ZMX backend.
- [Connectors (Webhook)](/botmux/en/webhook.md): <video src="../img/video-v5-automation-en.mp4" controls preload="metadata" style="width:100%;border-radius:8px"></video> A connector lets an external system (monitoring alerts, CI, tickets, scheduled scripts…) put a bot to work through a URL: send one HTTP POST and the bot reads the event in a group and handles it. botmux doesn't parse each platform's format. It hands the JSON it receives to the model as-is, so connecting a new system usually just means pasting the URL in. Create and manage connectors in the Dashboard under "Management → Webhook". The "Invocation logs" tab on the same page shows the result of every call.
- [Local Whiteboard](/botmux/en/whiteboard.md): The whiteboard is a markdown note stored on your machine. All bots and sessions in the same Feishu group share one. It records where the project stands right now: goals, roles, approach, progress, next steps. When a new session or a different bot takes over, the agent reads the whiteboard and catches up without scrolling through chat history. Useful for multi-agent work, resuming long tasks, and handing off across topics. The whiteboard is a snapshot, not a log: every update rewrites the whole thing as the latest state. Old content is not kept. Off by default. While off, no boards are created, no sessions are bound, nothing is added to prompts, and agent read/write commands are rejected.
- [Agent Workbench](/botmux/en/workbench.md): <video src="../img/video-v7-dashboard-en.mp4" controls preload="metadata" style="width:100%;border-radius:8px"></video> The Workbench (shown as 驾驶舱, "Cockpit", in the Dashboard) is the part of the Dashboard built for keeping an eye on many AI sessions at once: the left side lists every session on this machine, the right side shows the terminal of the one you pick. You can see at a glance which session just finished and which one is stuck waiting for you. The "Open Workbench" button on the Lark /dashboard card and the 工作台: … link printed by botmux dashboard both open it. Good for: Running several topics at once and wanting to know who's done and who's waiting on you, without digging through Lark groups.Watching a session's live terminal, and typing into it when needed.A quick progress check from your phone.
- [Workflow (experimental)](/botmux/en/workflow.md): Workflow turns a goal that takes several steps into a flow that runs on its own: the bot first asks you questions, one at a time, until the requirement is clear;it then compiles the requirement into a DAG (a step graph with dependencies; each step is a "node");once you confirm, it runs automatically, with independent steps in parallel;a flow that worked can be saved as a Saved Workflow and rerun with one command. It fits tasks with a clear end and one deliverable, like "research three competitors and produce a comparison report" or "pull the logs, analyze them, and make charts". You don't need it for single-step questions or ordinary code changes, and it is not meant for long-running projects where several bots keep splitting and coordinating work.
- [ZMX Session Backend](/botmux/en/zmx.md): ZMX is a lightweight terminal session manager. With ZMX as the botmux session backend, the CLI runs inside a ZMX session process: it survives daemon restarts, and you can zmx attach from a local terminal at any time to keep working with the full terminal UI. First, check whether it fits: ZMX is explicit opt-in: botmux does not install it, and finding zmx on PATH never makes botmux pick it automatically.
